title: Neither coming nor going (section 29)
hookLine: the Tathagata neither comes nor goes; that is why he is called the Tathagata

cards: A map app runs on two questions. Where are you? Where are you going?

A blue dot, a line, a time to arrival, and at the end a cheerful voice: you have arrived. A few minutes later, a new destination. Whole days can be lived inside that blue dot, always on the way, rarely there.
The Diamond Sutra opened with the Buddha on the move, walking into town for alms and back again. Now, near the end, section twenty-nine seems to erase the whole walk.

teach.h: COMES, GOES, STANDS, SITS, LIES DOWN.
teach.b: The Buddha tells Subhuti, in paraphrase: if anyone says the Tathagata comes or goes, or stands, or sits, or lies down, that person hasn't understood what I teach.
Those are the ordinary shapes of a body's day, and the Tathagata isn't to be pinned to any of them.
But we watched him do every one. Back in section one he walked to town with his bowl, ate, came back, washed his feet and sat down. The sutra isn't taking that back.
The body walked. The question is whether the one called Tathagata is that walking.
The sutra's reason: the Tathagata doesn't go anywhere and doesn't come from anywhere, and that is exactly why he is called the Tathagata. The sutra hands the title its own meaning.
Not a traveler who arrived somewhere special, not a visitor who will one day leave. What the name points to was never on the road.

It's the cut from the verse about form and sound, one step deeper: not the body's shape, and not its movements either. So much of a life is spent in transit, in the head if not on the road. Almost there.
Not yet. Next. Section twenty-nine doesn't tell anyone to stop walking.

teach.h: STILL IN THE MIDDLE OF THE WALK.
teach.b: The dishes still need doing and the bus still leaves at eight.
It points at something in the middle of all the walking that isn't going anywhere.

how: Mahayana Buddhists who study the Diamond Sutra read section 29 as the sutra's own gloss on the title Tathagata.

games.q: what does “neither coming nor going” mean?
o: a rule that monks must never travel far from home
the Tathagata goes nowhere and comes from nowhere
a monk who stays in one place for the rainy season

games.q: neither coming nor going: tap the pairs.
p: the Buddha walks to town for alms

s: section 29 denies that the Buddha ever walked anywhere
section 1 shows him walking for alms; section 29 says the one called Tathagata isn't that walking.
the sutra gives the title Tathagata its own meaning here
he goes nowhere and comes from nowhere; that is why he's called Tathagata.
the sutra tells practitioners to stop moving
it doesn't forbid walking; it points to what isn't going anywhere in the middle of it.

games.q: someone says: the Tathagata came to town, then went back to the grove. what does section 29 say about that person?
o: they should add that he sat down
games.why: anyone who says the Tathagata comes, goes, stands, sits or lies down hasn't understood: he goes nowhere and comes from nowhere.

practice: Notice where your mind is headed: the next task, tonight, tomorrow, the blue dot moving. Then let the destination go for a moment; the breath comes, the breath goes, and the knowing of it stays right here.
If the mind leaves for somewhere, notice it went, and come back without scolding.

wordCard.voice: Neither coming nor going. Section twenty-nine: the Tathagata goes nowhere and comes from nowhere, and that is why he is called the Tathagata. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit and Pali: the title the Buddha uses for himself; section 29 explains it as one who neither comes nor goes.

carryVoice: Your line: neither coming nor going. Nowhere this breath has to take you. Day one thousand one hundred forty-six, and you're right here.
